title: Hardware + QPS sweep: trace-level p50/p95/p99 per-stage decomposition
body:
Summary:

This is the working write-up for the hardware x QPS sweep we ran 2025-11-02 -> 2025-11-03 focused on end-to-end trace-level latency decomposition. Goal was to quantify which pipeline stages dominate at different load points and across GPU families, and to validate that our autoscaler + routing keeps p95/p99 within SLOs under controlled bursts.

Test matrix (executed):
- GPUs: T4 (32GB), A100-40GB, H100-80GB (dedicated pools)
- Model: open-mix-medium-v2 (seq_len 1024), default kv-cache behavior (warm vs cold runs)
- Quantization: FP16 baseline, int8-opt trial on A100/H100 nodes
- QPS points: 10, 50, 200, 500 (single-pod), 2k (multi-pod across dedicated pool)
- Batch configs: batching disabled (latency-first), batching enabled (max-batch 8), and continuous-batching experimental mode
- Warmup: 1000 warm requests before sampling traces for each point
- Number of traces collected per condition: 500 (random sample)

Methodology / instrumentation:
- Collected full distributed traces (ingress -> routing -> pod accept -> model engine stages -> egress). Traces were sampled at 10% during low-QPS and 100% during high-QPS bursts for better p99 visibility.
- Per-stage spans: http_recv, auth/rate_limit, routing/dispatch, pod_enqueue, pod_startup (cold model init), kv_cache_lookup, decoder_attention (token-loop cumulative), token_emit, http_send.
- Derived metrics: per-request cumulative decode time (sum of decoder_attention spans), queuing time (pod_enqueue -> pod_start), model compute (pod_start -> kv_lookup -> decode end), network overhead (http_recv + http_send).
- Traces correlated with node-level metrics (GPU util, SM clocks, host CPU, thrift queue lengths) and runtime logs for KV cache hits.

Key findings (high level):
1) For low QPS (10-50) on A100/H100 with warm KV cache, p50/p95 dominated by model compute (decoder_attention) and had low queuing; p99 often impacted by occasional GC/heap compaction in Python shim on a subset of pods (~2-3% pods).
2) At medium QPS (200) with batching disabled: A100 p95 stayed < 120ms but p99 rose to ~260ms due to transient queuing spikes; H100 improved p99 by ~20% consistently. T4 had much wider tail (p99 ~720ms) due to slower attention kernels and more frequent polyfill fallbacks.
3) At high single-pod QPS (500): queuing became the largest contributor to p95/p99 on all GPU types when batching disabled. Enabling batching (max-batch 8) reduced p95 by 22–36% at the cost of ~15ms p50 increase.
4) Multi-pod (2k QPS) introduced cross-pod routing variance: routing/dispatch + pod_accept latency contributed ~30–40% of p99 when autoscaler had not yet added pods. Once autoscale converged, model compute regained dominance.
5) Cold KV cache runs (first request after pod startup) add ~120–300ms per-request (kv_cache_lookup + model warm path); this is a persistent source of outliers for p99 in bursty traffic.
6) Int8-opt quantization on A100/H100 reduced decoder_attention compute by ~28% median, and improved p99 by ~18% on A100; on T4 int8 path triggered software fallback in 13% of traces, worsening p99.

Representative numbers (selected rows from aggregated trace table) - warm KV, batching disabled:
- A100 @ 50 QPS: p50=42ms, p95=88ms, p99=170ms
  - breakdown p50/p95/p99 (model_compute=70%/64%/52%, queuing=5%/10%/16%, routing=8%/9%/12%, network=17%/17%/20%)
- H100 @ 200 QPS: p50=35ms, p95=98ms, p99=210ms
  - breakdown (model_compute=76%/70%/60%, queuing=6%/14%/22%, routing=9%/8%/10%, network=9%/8%/8%)
- T4 @ 200 QPS: p50=120ms, p95=430ms, p99=720ms
  - breakdown (model_compute=82%/76%/68%, queuing=8%/12%/18%, routing=3%/4%/6%, network=7%/8%/8%)

Stage-level notes and examples from traces:
- pod_enqueue -> pod_start: High variance observed when pod CPU saturated handling async IO (python event loop stalls). Example trace id trace-20251103-A100-5321 shows 180ms enqueue->start due to thread pool contention on shard-3.
- kv_cache_lookup: Cold misses cost ~120–300ms; partial warm where cache has prefix but not full k-v chain can still add ~60–90ms due to extra device-host synchronizations.
- decoder_attention: The token loop remains the single biggest cost under steady state. Profiling of kernel launch times shows longer tail when sequence length spikes above 768; attention kernel re-allocs cause 10–25ms jitter.
- routing/dispatch: We saw ~12ms median for local pod dispatch, but cross-availability-zone dispatch jumps to 40–120ms p99. This surfaces in multi-AZ dedicated pools.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Python shim GC spikes are a major contributor to sporadic p99s at low-medium QPS: suspect large ephemeral allocations in telemetry/enrichment hooks. (Priority: P0)
2) Queuing spikes at 200–500 QPS are caused by suboptimal IO thread pool sizing + blocking hooks in request path; increasing async worker pool and converting enrichment to background tasks should reduce p99. (Priority: P0)
3) T4 regression is due to falling back to slower kernels for int8 and sequence lengths >512; switch to A100/H100 recommendation for heavy production. (Priority: P1)
4) Routing variance in multi-pod runs is amplified by autoscaler step delay; faster scale or pre-warmed burst capacity would reduce windowed p99s. (Priority: P1)

Action items / next experiments:
- Short term (this week):
  - Instrument and add a lightweight allocation profiler to Python shim to verify GC/alloc hotspots (owner: Marco).
  - Increase async IO worker pool for serving runtime on a canary subset and re-run 200/500 QPS to measure p99 impact (owner: Leah).
  - Disable int8 fallback path on T4 nodes for production routing until the software path is verified; add guardrail in routing policy (owner: Daniel).

- Medium term (2–4 weeks):
  - Implement per-pod warmup option in autoscaler: keep N standing warm pods to absorb short bursts; run cost vs SLO trade analysis.
  - Add sequence-length aware kernel selection heuristic to runtime so that for sequences >512 we pick a different kernel path to avoid re-alloc jitter.
  - Explore moving enrichment telemetry to async post-emit pipeline to avoid blocking decode loop.

Commands / queries used (notes for reproducibility):
- Trace query (example):
  - internal-trace-query --service=serving-runtime --tag=hw-sweep-20251103 --percentiles=50,95,99 --group-by=stage
- Node metrics correlation:
  - kubectl top node --selector=pool=dedicated-a100 | jq ...
  - gpustat --json /metrics | tee gpu-metrics-a100-200qps.json

Open questions:
- What's the root cause of the Python shim allocations? Are we pulling large tensors into host memory for logging?
- Can we accept small p50 regressions to get big p99 wins via batching or pre-warmed pods? Define acceptable trade-off for PLG use-cases.
- For int8 on T4, is the root cause kernel availability or a bug in our quant runner?

Appendix: quick sample trace snippets (abstracted):
- trace-20251103-A100-5321: http_recv 3ms | routing 11ms | pod_enqueue 6ms | pod_start 180ms | kv_cache_lookup 8ms | decoder_attention 28ms | token_emit 2ms | http_send 4ms
- trace-20251103-T4-4112: http_recv 5ms | routing 15ms | pod_enqueue 22ms | pod_start 40ms | kv_cache_lookup 5ms | decoder_attention 610ms | token_emit 7ms | http_send 10ms

Notes for the doc reviewer:
- This is a mid-draft: numbers are aggregated from 500-sample slices per condition; raw traces and the full spreadsheet are linked in linked_artifacts.
- Please review hypotheses and flag any missing experiment permutations (e.g., cold-start distribution across AZs).
summary_title: Short summary for execs: A100/H100 are within SLO at moderate QPS; tails driven by queuing and python shim GC; T4 shows wide tails and less reliable int8 speedups.
